title: Linux OOM Killer Tuning, overcommit_memory, and PostgreSQL Work_mem
realWorldScenario: Without warning, the primary PostgreSQL instance abruptly shuts down during month-end reporting. Kernel syslog shows: `Out of Memory: Killed process 4102 (postgres) total-vm: 64GB, anon-rss: 58GB`. After restart, the database went through a 15-minute crash recovery.
questionStatement: Analyze how Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer interacts with PostgreSQL memory management. Explain `shared_buffers` vs `work_mem` multiplication per connection, Linux `vm.overcommit_memory`, `vm.overcommit_ratio`, and how to configure `oom_score_adj` to protect the PostgreSQL postmaster.

symptoms: Sudden total database crash and connection drop
Kernel dmesg: Out of Memory: Killed process
Dozens of complex analytical queries running concurrently

systemTelemetry.logSnippet:
kernel: [89104.12] Out of memory: Kill process 4102 (postgres) score 852 or sacrifice child
kernel: [89104.14] Killed process 4102 (postgres) total-vm:67108864kB, anon-rss:61440000kB
postgres[101]: [1-1] LOG:  server process (PID 4102) was terminated by signal 9: Killed
postgres[101]: [2-1] LOG:  terminating any other active server processes
postgres[101]: [3-1] LOG:  all server processes terminated; reinitializing shared memory and database

candidateTasks: Explain why Linux killed postmaster or backend child with SIGKILL (signal 9)
Demonstrate how work_mem * max_connections causes RAM oversubscription
Configure oom_score_adj = -1000 for the main postmaster process

expectedConcepts: Linux OOM killer killing processes with SIGKILL (signal 9)
Shared memory corruption risk forcing database restart
work_mem allocated per operation per connection (multiplication factor)
hints: Is work_mem allocated once per connection, or once per sort/hash operation in a query?
What happens when Linux kills a backend process holding shared buffers?
